<h1>Organizing and Converting</h1>
<p>Create a file system that makes every accelerometer file traceable to the participant, batch, software setting, and processing decision that produced it.</p>

::: {.lesson-main}

::: {.review-note}
<strong>Module guide:</strong> Bring a fictional or de-identified inventory of raw files; do not move or rename the only copy of study data while learning. The concept route requires only the examples and self-check. For the hands-on route, work in a practice folder. Your deliverable is a folder map, naming convention, batch log, and written conversion decision. You are finished when a second analyst can trace every practice file from its raw source to its processing status.
:::

::: {.objectives-panel}
<p class="section-kicker">Learning outcomes</p>
<h2>By the end of this module, you should be able to:</h2>

1. Build a transparent folder structure for raw, converted, processed, and final files.
2. Apply consistent file-naming rules and batch logs.
3. Convert ActiGraph files in ActiLife when conversion is needed.
4. Explain why `.gt3x` to `.csv` conversion is pipeline-dependent rather than universally required.
:::

::: {.lesson-section #folder-structure}
<p class="section-kicker">Lesson 3.1</p>
<h2>Folder Structure</h2>

Use a folder structure that separates raw evidence from files created later in the pipeline. A simple structure is:

```text
accelerometer_project/
  01_raw_downloads/
    batch_001/
      COMPLETE/
      INCOMPLETE/
  02_converted_files/
  03_ggir_input/
  04_ggir_output/
  05_qc_review/
  06_cleaned_data/
  07_stata_final/
  logs/
```

Raw downloads should be treated as read-only after the first handoff. If a file must be renamed, keep a log linking the original file name, new study ID, device ID, download batch, and operator.

::: {.cohort-example}
<strong>Worked example: Pelotas/UFPel cohort</strong><br>
Separate each collection lot or batch before processing. Keep the original raw downloads, the conversion outputs, and GGIR outputs in different folders. This makes it possible to append lots later in Stata without losing the batch history.
:::

::: {.learning-activity}
<strong>Mini-activity: sketch the project folders</strong>
<p>Copy the example tree and annotate who can write to each folder, which folders are backed up, and which files are treated as read-only evidence.</p>

<details>
<summary>Check your folder map</summary>

The original downloads should be preserved and separated from converted, processed, cleaned, and final files. Logs should connect these stages. A defensible map also identifies a backup location and prevents routine processing from overwriting raw evidence.

</details>
:::
:::

::: {.lesson-section #naming-and-batch-logs}
<p class="section-kicker">Lesson 3.2</p>
<h2>Naming and Batch Logs</h2>

Every file should be traceable to:

1. participant or study ID,
2. device serial number,
3. collection lot/batch,
4. download date,
5. operator,
6. file format and processing status.

Avoid names such as `participant1.csv` or `newfile.gt3x`. Prefer a naming pattern such as:

```text
studyid_batch_deviceid_YYYYMMDD_raw.gt3x
studyid_batch_deviceid_YYYYMMDD_converted.csv
```

The exact pattern can differ across studies; the important rule is that another analyst can reconstruct where each file came from.

::: {.learning-activity}
<strong>Mini-activity: test a naming rule</strong>
<p>Rename three fictional records using your proposed pattern, including two batches and two device IDs. Then check whether sorting by file name preserves the distinctions your team needs.</p>

<details>
<summary>Feedback</summary>

A useful name is unique, stable, machine-friendly, and supported by a log. Avoid direct identifiers, spaces, ambiguous dates, and status words that may later change. If a file is renamed, the log must preserve both the original and new names.

</details>
:::
:::

::: {.lesson-section #actilife-conversion}
<p class="section-kicker">Lesson 3.3</p>
<h2>ActiLife Conversion Workflow</h2>

Some workflows convert ActiGraph files to `.csv` for software that cannot read `.gt3x`. If conversion is part of the approved workflow, use a batch process rather than manual one-by-one exports.

Recommended ActiLife conversion steps:

1. Open **ActiLife**.
2. Go to **File -> Import/Export/Convert**.
3. Choose **RAW to RAW**.
4. Select **GT3X -> CSV (batch)**.
5. Select the input folder containing `.gt3x` files.
6. For the documented GGIR raw-CSV export, set **TimeStamps** to **Off**, as required by GGIR's ActiGraph CSV guidance. For any other downstream workflow, confirm and document its schema rather than copying this setting automatically.
7. Check **create subfolder** so converted files are separated from the originals.
8. Run the batch conversion and save the conversion log.

Menu labels and defaults can differ by ActiLife version. Record the version used and verify the current documentation before converting study files.

::: {.lesson-section #conversion-necessity}
<p class="section-kicker">Lesson 3.4</p>
<h2>Is Conversion Always Necessary?</h2>

No. GGIR can directly read `.gt3x` files, so converting `.gt3x` to `.csv` is not required for the GGIR pipeline taught in Module 4. Conversion is useful only when a downstream script, external software package, data-sharing requirement, or audit workflow specifically needs `.csv`.

::: {.review-note}
<strong>Pipeline decision:</strong> Convert only if the approved downstream workflow requires CSV. For the GGIR path in this course, preserve `.gt3x` as the raw input and document any additional export separately.
:::

If a batch begins with 100 `.gt3x` files and every file converts once, expect 100 original raw files plus 100 converted outputs in separate locations. Reconcile the input count, successful-output count, failed conversions, duplicate names, and log before processing.
:::

::: {.lesson-section #knowledge-check}
<p class="section-kicker">Wrap-up</p>
<h2>Self-Check</h2>

1. Why should raw downloads be kept separate from converted and processed files?
2. GGIR is the only planned downstream tool and it accepts the available `.gt3x` files. Should the team batch-convert them to CSV?
3. A batch contains 100 raw files, 99 successful outputs, and one error. What should happen next?
4. Which records make a renamed file traceable?

<details>
<summary>Feedback and suggested answers</summary>

1. Separation preserves the original evidence, prevents accidental overwrite, and makes each transformation auditable.
2. No conversion is needed for that reason alone. Keep `.gt3x` as the GGIR input unless another documented requirement justifies an export.
3. Stop before routine processing, identify the failed file, preserve the error, retry only through the documented procedure, and reconcile the log and counts.
4. At minimum, preserve the original and new names, study ID, device ID, batch, date, operator, file format, and reason for the change.

</details>
